title: C# and .NET Foundations: Typed Models to an Async Progress Tracker
description: A beginner C# course covering the .NET build model, types, nullable references, patterns, collections, LINQ, methods, records, classes, JSON, async I/O, and a tested progress-tracker capstone.
prerequisites: Ability to create and save a text file
learningOutcomes: Build and diagnose nullable-enabled .NET console applications
Use typed control flow, generic collections, LINQ, methods, records, and encapsulated classes
Build an async JSON-backed progress tracker with runtime validation and tests

lessons.title: The .NET Build and Execution Model
lessons.summary: Create a .NET console project and understand source, compilation, assemblies, the runtime, entry points, diagnostics, and repeatable builds.
objectives: Explain and apply The .NET Build and Execution Model
Use compiler and runtime evidence to test the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: The .NET SDK supplies `dotnet new`, `dotnet build`, `dotnet run`, and testing tools. C# source is compiled into an assembly containing intermediate language and metadata; the .NET runtime loads and executes it. A project file selects the target framework and dependencies. Treat warnings as design feedback, enable nullable analysis, and read the earliest relevant diagnostic rather than changing unrelated code. `dotnet run` builds when needed, but explicit `dotnet build` is useful when separating compiler evidence from runtime behavior.

lessons.title: Types, Conversion, and Nullable References
lessons.summary: Use value and reference types, type inference, strings, parsing, nullable reference analysis, and explicit handling of absent values.
objectives: Explain and apply Types, Conversion, and Nullable References
Use compiler and runtime evidence to test the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: C# is statically typed. `var` asks the compiler to infer one fixed type from the initializer; it is not dynamic typing. Numeric conversions can be implicit when safe or explicit when information may be lost. Prefer `TryParse` for expected user-input failure. With nullable reference types enabled, `string` means non-null and `string?` admits null. Narrow a nullable value with a null check, pattern, or `??` default before dereferencing. The null-forgiving operator `!` suppresses analysis but performs no runtime validation, so it requires independent evidence.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: `if` chains suit numeric ranges, while switch expressions provide concise exhaustive mappings for finite cases. `&&` and `||` short-circuit, protecting later expressions from invalid state. Pattern matching can test type, null, property, and relational evidence while introducing narrowed variables. Use parentheses when mixed operators obscure intent. A switch over an enum should handle every expected value; a discard arm should be intentional rather than hiding missing domain cases. Test below, at, and above each threshold.

lessons.title: Collections, Iteration, and LINQ
lessons.summary: Use arrays, List, Dictionary, HashSet, foreach, generic types, and LINQ without hiding mutation or repeated enumeration.
objectives: Explain and apply Collections, Iteration, and LINQ
Use compiler and runtime evidence to test the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Arrays have fixed length; `List<T>` provides an ordered resizable sequence; `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` maps unique keys; `HashSet<T>` enforces uniqueness. Generics preserve element types. `foreach` expresses value traversal, while an indexed loop is appropriate when position matters. LINQ operators such as `Where`, `Select`, and `Average` describe queries and often use deferred execution, meaning results may reflect later source changes. Materialize with `ToList` when a stable snapshot is required. Do not structurally modify a collection during its enumeration.

objectives: Explain and apply Methods, Records, Classes, and Encapsulation
Use compiler and runtime evidence to test the contract

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Methods declare input and output contracts. Use optional parameters sparingly and place them after required parameters. C# passes arguments by value unless `ref`, `out`, or `in` is explicit; reference-type values still identify shared objects. Records are useful for value-oriented data, while classes suit identity and encapsulated mutable behavior. Keep setters private when updates require validation. Constructors should establish valid state, and public methods must preserve it. Throw specific exceptions for violated programming contracts and use result-style handling for expected user mistakes.

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: `using` and `await using` ensure disposable resources are released. High-level file APIs simplify small text operations, while streams suit larger or incremental data. Treat JSON as untrusted: deserialization can produce null or domain-invalid values, so validate before accepting state. `async` methods usually return `Task` or `Task<T>` and should be awaited; `async void` is reserved for event handlers. Pass cancellation tokens through cancellable operations. Keep I/O at the boundary and domain calculations synchronous and testable.
